h1: What changes when a brewpub becomes a production brewery
title: Brewpub to Production Brewery | Craft Beer School
desc: What changes when a brewpub becomes a production brewery in India: licence, packaging, quality, cold chain and working capital, with a cash sum.
teaser: A brewpub sells beer in days to people standing next to the tank. A production brewery sells it in months to people it never meets.
standfirst: Moving from a brewpub to a production brewery changes the licence, the quality system, the packaging and the way cash moves. The beer is the same. The business around it is not. Here is what changes and the order to deal with it.
sections:
A brewpub brews, serves and sells in one building. Beer travels a few metres, is drunk within days and is sold at a full retail price. A production brewery packs beer, sends it through a distributor or retailer and waits to be paid. It earns a wholesale price, not a retail one. It also carries stock, packaging and receivables that a brewpub never sees.

Owners who treat the move as 'brewpub, but bigger' tend to find out the difference at the first rejected pallet or the first late payment. Plan for it as a different business.
The licence is the first gate

In India, a brewpub or microbrewery licence and a production licence are different categories. Alcohol is a state subject, so rules, fees and conditions vary by state and change. Typical steps include premises approval, a licence for manufacture, brand and label registration and arrangements for movement and sale. Some states have tight rules on where a brewpub can sell beer outside its own premises.

We do not quote fees or section numbers. Work with a licensing consultant and read our guide to getting a factory licence for a production brewery for the process. Start early, because approvals set your timeline more than equipment does.

A brewpub pours fresh beer from a tank. A production brewery must make beer that survives weeks or months in a package. That raises the bar in four places:

  • Oxygen. Total package oxygen needs to be very low, measured in parts per billion. Hop-forward beer needs the lowest figures of all. Oxygen is what turns a fresh beer to cardboard in a warm shop.
  • Microbiology. A single wild yeast that is harmless in a tank can over-carbonate a can in the warehouse.
  • Stability. Haze, colour and foam must hold for the declared shelf life.
  • Labelling. Brand names, strength, batch numbers and dates all need to match the registered label.

This means a lab, even a small one: dissolved oxygen, plating or PCR checks, a refractometer and a density meter. Our guide to brewpub vs microbrewery covers the earlier fork.
The floor detail: the first shelf-life trial

Before you sell a single can, run a shelf-life trial. Pack three batches. Hold samples at the temperature they will meet in a warm warehouse and a shop, around 30 °C. Keep a cold control. Taste and measure each at 2, 4, 8 and 12 weeks. You are looking for the point where the beer stops tasting like your reference. That date, minus a safety margin, becomes your best-before date. Many beers that taste perfect at the pub are tired at week six.

The distributor, the state warehouse, the retailer and the bar all handle the beer. Each can add heat. Decide early how you will move kegs and cans, who owns the truck and who is accountable when a pallet sits in the sun. Hop-forward beers suffer most. A lager survives more abuse.

Price the beer from the other end. The retail price in the shop, minus the retailer's share, the distributor's share, state levies and your logistics, leaves what you earn per litre. In many states the margin structure is set by notification, so check the current one instead of copying another brewery's price list.
Cash: the part that surprises owners

A brewpub gets paid at the table. A production brewery gets paid weeks later. Here is an illustration with round, made-up numbers. Suppose daily cash costs are ₹60,000. You hold 30 days of stock and packaging, wait 45 days to be paid and pay your suppliers in 20 days.

Working capital needed = (30 + 45 - 20) x 60,000 = 55 x 60,000 = ₹33,00,000.

That money is tied up before you earn a rupee of margin. It is a loan from your bank or your shareholders. It grows with every extra pallet. Use your own days and costs. Do the sum before you sign for equipment. Our guide to opening a second brewpub outlet shows the alternative route to growth that keeps more cash in hand.

A production brewery needs people a brewpub does not: a quality lead, a packaging line operator, a store keeper, a logistics coordinator and someone who owns compliance records. Batch records, calibration logs and recall plans move from nice-to-have to essential. If a retailer asks which batch a can came from, you need an answer in minutes.

Write the procedures before the first run. A line with no cleaning schedule fails its first microbiology test.

The move can be right, but only if the numbers hold after you add packaging, logistics, working capital and compliance. Build a model with those costs in it, test it against a pessimistic case and decide on the lower number. That kind of costing and planning is where a brewer's instinct needs a business framework behind it.
faqs: Is a production brewery licence different from a brewpub licence in India?
Usually yes. Categories, fees and conditions differ by state and change, so check the current notification or ask a licensing consultant.
What is the biggest financial change from a brewpub to a production brewery?
Working capital. You hold stock, wait for payment and pay suppliers, so cash is tied up before margin arrives. Do the sum for your own days.
Do I need a lab for a production brewery?
Yes, at least a small one. You need oxygen, microbiology and basic analysis to be sure packaged beer survives its shelf life.
